hero.text: 12 practical articles from English Teaching Forum, chosen for classrooms like ours: large, mixed-ability and short of materials. Each has a summary, notes for a Sri Lankan classroom, and the full article to read.

blocks.heading: About these articles
text: English Teaching Forum is a free quarterly journal for English teachers, published by the U.S. Department of State and distributed in more than a hundred countries. Most of its authors are classroom teachers, and its articles are practical: an activity, a routine, a way of managing a class.

We have chosen the ones that work where classes are large, books are shared and a lesson lasts forty minutes. For each there is a short summary, the steps, a note on using it in a Sri Lankan classroom, and the whole article, which you can read on the page or open on your phone.

basedOn.title: Student-Centered Teaching in Large Classes with Limited Resources

hero.text: Classes of 50 to 80, no textbooks and a piece of chalk: what still works, tested by the teachers themselves.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Written from years of training English teachers in Haiti, where a class of 80 pupils on benches, with no books and no electricity, is ordinary. The authors define a large class as 50 to 80 and set out what can still be done there. The ideas were tried by the teachers themselves, in their own classrooms, and kept only if they worked.

The article is organised around four problems every teacher of a big class knows: keeping order, getting pupils to work together, teaching without materials, and holding the attention of pupils at very different levels.

items.definition: Susan Renaud, Elizabeth Tannenbaum and Phillip Stantial
English Teaching Forum, Volume 45, Number 3 (2007), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Let the class write the rules.** Groups draft rules and consequences, the class votes, and the final list stays on the wall all year. Rules pupils made are rules pupils keep.
**Build routines and a silent signal.** Agree a signal for quiet - a raised hand, a bell - and never try to shout over the room.
**Save time on the register.** A sign-in sheet passed along the rows, or folded name cards collected at the end of each lesson, takes attendance and teaches you names.
**Cut the marking.** Groups produce one piece of writing between them, and every piece is self-checked and peer-checked before it reaches you.
**Make group work quick to set up.** Pupils work with whoever sits beside or behind them; groups stay together for several lessons, with roles that rotate.
**Replace copying from the board.** A dictogloss - pupils hear a short text twice, then rebuild it in pairs - puts the same notes in their books with far more thinking.
**Plan for the fast finishers.** Keep extra tasks ready, and use stronger pupils as helpers.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: This is the article to start with. Its classrooms are larger and poorer than most in Sri Lanka, so almost everything in it transfers - the bench seating, the lack of copies, the pupils who need something to do while others finish.

The marking advice matters most in the O/L years, when every writing task multiplies by forty. One group paragraph, checked by the group first, is far more feedback than forty paragraphs returned late.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Agree a silent signal with the class and practise it three times.
Take the register with a passed-round sheet and see how much of the lesson it saves.

basedOn.title: Minimizing the Chaos through Cooperative Classroom Management

hero.text: Four colour-coded jobs in every group - and the noise, the drift and the one pupil who does all the talking are handled by the pupils.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: An experienced teacher trainer describes her first week with a large class of Moroccan teacher-trainees: group work that was too loud to hear, impossible to monitor, and dominated by a few voices. Her answer was not less group work but more organisation - and handing part of the running of the class to the pupils.
The heart of the article is a way of giving every group member a colour and a job, so that every pupil speaks, the volume stays down and the talk stays in English.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 51, Number 4 (2013), U.S. Department of State
Morocco, where the author trained high-school English teachers

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Collect a card from every pupil** on the first day, with the name they want to be called. Use the cards to form mixed groups of four.
**Mark the cards** with a letter for each group a pupil has been in, so that new groups can be formed quickly without repeating old ones.
**Give each group member a colour** - red, orange, yellow, green. Calling out a colour ("All the greens, stand up") gets an answer from every group without anyone volunteering.
**Attach a job to each colour:** red keeps the group on topic, orange keeps the volume down, yellow keeps the talk in English, green makes sure everyone takes part. Rotate the jobs each week.
**Let the class decide the expectations and the consequences** - for example, a pupil who keeps slipping out of English stands for two minutes. Because pupils set them, they are seldom needed.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: Colours solve a problem every Sri Lankan teacher has met: the same few hands going up. When "the yellows" are asked to report, every group has to produce someone, and the quiet pupil has been warned in advance.

The language monitor works even with weak classes if two phrases are taught first: "How do you say ... in English?" and "What does ... mean?" Pupils can then stay in English while asking for the English.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Number the four seats in each group with colours and ask one colour to report back.
Give one pupil in each group the volume job for the lesson.

basedOn.title: Group Progress Charts for Young Learners

hero.text: By a lecturer at Mahaweli National College of Education, Kandy: roles for every pupil and a wall chart that lets the whole group climb towards a goal together.

blocks.title: Written in Sri Lanka
text: This article is by a Sri Lankan teacher educator, about Sri Lankan classrooms, published in an international journal distributed to English teachers in more than a hundred countries.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Written by Malka N. Wickramasinghe, a senior lecturer in English teacher education at Mahaweli National College of Education in Kandy. Her trainee teachers found on their first practicum that they could not hold a class's attention. In mixed-ability groups the stronger pupils did the task while the rest drifted.

Her solution has two parts. First, every pupil in a group has a role - leader, writer, presenter, and invented ones that suit the topic. Then a progress chart on the wall shows each group moving step by step towards a goal as it completes each task, so every pupil is needed to move the group on.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 60, Number 2 (2022), U.S. Department of State
Sri Lanka: the author is a senior lecturer in English pre-service teacher education at Mahaweli National College of Education, Kandy

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Introduce roles over a few lessons** until pupils are used to them. Tie new roles to the topic - for a lesson on the environment, a head of department, a media secretary, field officers.
**Add a "spy"** who visits other groups to clear up instructions, then brings the answers back while the group starts on easier tasks.

**Make the chart:** one column for each group, divided into steps, with a group symbol that moves up as tasks are completed. A theme the class knows makes it more exciting - a race, a rescue, a butterfly climbing to a garden.
**Set tasks that step up in difficulty,** from filling blanks and true-or-false to questions that need explanation.
**Move each group up the chart** as it succeeds, and carry the quest over to the next lesson if it runs long.
**Stress that every group can finish.** The chart is there to drive the group, not to crown a winner.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: This one is ours - written in and for Sri Lankan classrooms, and it shows. It needs only chart paper and markers, and it answers the practicum problem every training college knows.
It suits Grades 3 to 7 best, and fits the group activities already in the primary and junior secondary Pupil's Books: the book supplies the tasks, the chart supplies the reason to finish them.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Draw a four-step chart on the board with one column per group, and move a group up each time it completes a task.
Give every group member a named role before the next group activity.

basedOn.title: Using Practice Posters to Address EFL Challenges

hero.text: One poster of pictures and cue words, and in ten minutes a class practises fifty or more sentences before the lesson has really begun.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: A practice poster is a sheet of ten or twelve pictures, each with a short cue underneath - a name and a country, a job, a means of transport. The author, working in Mexico, used posters at the start of lessons to switch classes into English and to give every pupil a great deal of controlled speaking practice quickly.
The article sets out a ten-minute sequence, the benefits the author saw when using it, and the drawbacks to watch for.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 45, Number 3 (2007), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Make the poster:** pictures with cue words, on stiff card so it lasts.
**Drill the cues** with the whole class, then with groups and individuals.
**Model one statement** on the board from a cue and have pupils repeat it; pairs then make statements about the other pictures.
**Add the question form,** then the negative, each modelled and then practised in pairs.
**Hand the poster over** in later lessons: pupils lead their half of the class, or groups practise with different posters and swap.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: Posters answer two Sri Lankan problems at once: pupils who hear almost no English outside the lesson, and too few books to go round. One poster serves forty pupils, and pictures cut from newspapers or drawn by the class do the job.
It fits the grammar in the Grade 6 to 9 books well - be, have, present continuous, can - and makes a strong opening five or ten minutes to a PPP lesson.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Pin up six pictures with a cue word under each and run the question-and-answer sequence in pairs.

basedOn.title: Small Talks: Daily Speaking Practice for Vocabulary and Grammar Mastery

hero.text: A timed chat of under two minutes at the start of every lesson, on last lesson's words and grammar.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: A short daily routine from a Japanese middle school. At the start of each lesson, pupils talk in pairs on a simple topic for a fixed time - 40 seconds for beginners, up to two minutes for stronger classes - using the vocabulary or grammar from the previous lesson.

The article gives the procedure, lists of topics for weaker and stronger classes, and the small conversational phrases that keep a conversation going: showing interest, asking a follow-up question, changing the topic.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 59, Number 4 (2021), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Choose a topic** linked to the last lesson - my favourite food, a sport I can play.
**Put up the target words or structure,** and for weaker classes a model conversation.
**Teach a few conversation phrases** such as "Really? Why?" and "How about you?"
**Set the timer** and let pairs talk until it stops. Walk round and listen, but do not interrupt.
**Run a second round** with a new partner, perhaps reporting what the first partner said.
**Finish with two or three examples** you heard, correcting only mistakes in the target language.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: It fits inside a 40-minute period with room to spare, needs nothing but a watch, and turns the review that usually happens as questions to the class into talk by every pupil at once.

Start with the model conversation on the board for Grade 6 and 7 classes, and take it away after a week. In an O/L class the second round - reporting what a partner said - is useful practice in reported speech.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Open the next lesson with a one-minute pair chat on last lesson's grammar.

basedOn.title: Pair Counting to Improve Grammar and Spoken Fluency

hero.text: One partner talks for a minute, the other tallies every past-tense verb - then the talker tries to beat the score.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Pupils who write the past tense correctly often lose it when they speak, because their attention is on what they are saying. This short technique makes them watch one structure while they talk.

In pairs, one pupil talks for a minute on a prompt while the other counts how many times the target structure is used. The talker then speaks on the same topic again and tries to raise the count. The pair switch roles and repeat.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 55, Number 4 (2017), U.S. Department of State
EFL and ESL classes of teenagers and young adults

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Model it first:** talk for a minute yourself while the class tallies your past-tense verbs, then check the count together.
**Pair the class** into talkers and counters.
**Talkers speak for a minute** on a prompt such as "What did you do last weekend?" Counters tally the target verbs.
**Repeat the same topic** for the same time, aiming for a higher count.
**Switch roles.** Change the prompt to practise other structures - plans for the future, advice with should, everything in your bedroom.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: It needs only paper and a watch, keeps the whole class busy at once - half talking, half listening hard - and gives pupils a score to beat, which they like.

It suits the tense units in Grades 7 to 11 and the spoken tasks in the O/L syllabus. With a large class, check results by a show of hands with eyes closed rather than asking pupils to call out their numbers.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Pair the class and run two one-minute rounds on "What did you do yesterday?", counting past-tense verbs.

basedOn.title: A Good Listener Is a Good Speaker: Three Multisensory Activities

hero.text: Listening routines and three games - a memory chain, hidden sound-making objects and a number game - with notes on large classes.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Before pupils can speak well they have to listen well, and listening is a habit that has to be built. The article opens with short routines that settle a class for listening - a chant with gestures for younger pupils, a body-percussion rhythm for older ones.

It then describes three activities: a memory chain in which each speaker repeats what the last one said and adds their own; a game built around hidden objects that make sounds; and a number game. Each comes with variations for different ages and levels, including a version of the chain for large classes.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 63, Number 1 (2025), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Build a listening routine** that tells the class it is time to focus - the same chant or rhythm every time.
**The chain game:** each pupil repeats the previous sentence and adds a new one. In a large class, play in groups and have one member report the chain to the class.
**The vocabulary chain:** every pupil gets a cue card - "When you hear ..., you say ..." - so even shy pupils have one clear turn.
**The secret-object game:** pupils listen to hidden objects that make sounds, ask questions about them and draw what they think they are.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: Listening gets the least time in most Sri Lankan classrooms and carries marks in every examination paper. These activities give it a place without recordings or a speaker: the listening material is the class itself, and a few everyday objects that make a sound.
The vocabulary chain is especially useful with the shy pupil who never volunteers: the card tells them exactly when to speak and exactly what to say.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Teach a short listening chant and use it before every listening task for a week.

basedOn.title: Repeated Reading with Retelling: A Multi-Skilled Fluency Activity

hero.text: Two short texts, two partners: read aloud, take notes, retell in a minute, check - and repeat with a new partner.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Two well-known fluency activities have a weakness in common. In 4/3/2, pupils give the same talk three times in shrinking time, and in repeated reading they read the same easy text several times - but in neither is there much reason to communicate, and pupils can grow bored.

The author combines the two into one 20- to 30-minute activity. Partners hold different short texts. One reads aloud while the other takes notes and then retells it; the reader checks the retelling against the text. Because the listener needs every word, the reader cannot skim, and because the text is checked, the retelling has to be accurate.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 63, Number 3 (2025), U.S. Department of State
Any age, once pupils can read short simplified texts

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Choose two easy texts** of about 100 to 300 words, of similar length and on related topics. Pupil A has one, pupil B the other.
**Both read their own text silently** first.
**A reads aloud for three minutes** while B takes notes. If A finishes early, B asks for parts again.
**B retells A's text in one minute** from the notes. A checks it against the text.
**The pair fix what was missed** or misunderstood, then switch roles.
**Repeat with a new partner** once or twice, keeping the same texts. Notes are improved on each round.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: It turns the reading passages already in the Pupil's Book into speaking, listening and note-taking practice without a single photocopy - give the two halves of the class two different passages from the same unit.

The retelling step is direct practice for the summary and comprehension questions in the O/L paper, and pupils hear a correct model read aloud before each attempt, which matters where few hear English at home.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Split a Pupil's Book passage into two halves and run one round of read-note-retell in pairs.

basedOn.title: Better Writing with Big Paper: Peer Correction in Collaborative Learning Teams

hero.text: A pupil's uncorrected paragraph in the middle of a large sheet, and a group correcting it in silence, in writing.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Teachers argue about how much to correct pupils' writing: correct everything and pupils learn little, correct nothing and they learn less. This technique hands much of the correcting to the pupils, and makes them think while they do it.

A piece of a pupil's writing, not yet seen by the teacher, is stuck in the centre of a large sheet of paper. A small group gathers round it and, without speaking, writes comments on its spelling, grammar and punctuation - then comments on each other's comments. The finished sheets go up on the wall as a gallery.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 60, Number 2 (2022), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Prepare the paper:** flipchart or A3 sheets - or six A4 sheets taped together - and pens in different colours.
**Form groups of four** or five, and give each a name or a colour.
**Use writing pupils have already done** - a paragraph from homework, uncorrected by you - as the text in the middle.
**Work in silence:** each pupil writes corrections and comments round the text, marking their own comments with a colour or a shape so authorship is clear.
**Reply to each other's comments,** still in writing.
**Display the sheets** and let the class walk round and read them. In a class of thirty or more, larger groups take turns at the paper, which takes a little longer.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: It needs paper, pens and some tape, and it turns forty separate marking jobs into a handful of posters that the class has already corrected. Your part becomes checking the corrections, not making them.

Choose a paragraph that shows the errors the whole class is making - tense, articles, capital letters - and the poster teaches the point to everyone who reads it. It spreads over two lessons, so plan it into the unit rather than squeezing it into one period.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Pick one uncorrected homework paragraph and let a group of four correct it on a sheet of taped-together A4.

basedOn.title: The Single-Point Rubric to Simplify Student Feedback and Assessment

hero.text: One column of success criteria between two blank columns - one for what to improve, one for what was done well.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Rubrics make marking fairer, but the usual kinds have drawbacks: a single overall score tells the pupil little, and a full grid describing every level of every criterion takes a long time to write and to read.

A single-point rubric describes only what success looks like. The criteria sit in the middle column; the teacher writes on the left what still needs work and on the right how the pupil met or went beyond each one. The article shows how to write the learning objective and the criteria so that pupils can understand them and use the feedback before the final mark.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 63, Number 4 (2025), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Start from one clear objective,** written for pupils: "We will be able to ...", with an active verb and something that can be measured.
**List only a few criteria for success** - what a good piece of work does.
**Lay out three columns:** not yet met on the left, the criteria in the middle, how you met them on the right.
**Write short, specific comments** in the side columns rather than a score for each line.
**Share the rubric before the task,** so pupils know what they are aiming at.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: It suits School-Based Assessment well: a single-point rubric is quick to make for each SBA task, and the blank columns give each pupil a comment worth reading instead of a mark alone.
In a large class it saves time twice - fewer criteria to write, and feedback short enough to give in the lesson.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Write three success criteria for your next speaking or writing task and give pupils the three-column sheet before they start.

basedOn.title: Teaching beyond the Test: A Method for Designing Test-Preparation Classes

hero.text: Stop teaching exam tricks: find the skill each question type is testing, and teach that.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: Written by a former test developer, the article argues that exam "tricks" waste time. Modern examinations such as IELTS, TOEFL and PTE are built to measure real skills and are hard to coach, so the useful preparation is building those skills.

It sets three goals for a preparation class - know the test, build the skills it measures, and teach the language that supports them - and then shows, with one question type as an example, how to turn what a test measures into class objectives and activities.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 51, Number 4 (2013), U.S. Department of State

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Take one question type** from the examination.
**Ask what it claims to show** about a candidate - what they can do if they answer it well.
**Break that into sub-skills:** for a listening summary item, finding the main idea, following the main points, recognising the same idea said in different words.
**Write objectives** from the sub-skills and design activities for each.
**With weaker learners, take one objective at a time;** with stronger ones, combine several in one task.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: The examples are international tests, but the method is exactly what an O/L or A/L General English class needs. Every question on those papers is there to test a skill - reading for detail, writing a notice, summarising - and pupils drilled on past papers alone often learn the paper, not the skill.
It is equally useful to anyone preparing IELTS candidates, and the site's IELTS pages take the same approach, question type by question type.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Take one question from last year's paper and list the two or three skills it is really testing.

hero.text: A village primary teacher in Bangladesh who gets children speaking with chants, stories and games instead of memorisation.

blocks.heading: In brief
text: A profile of Asif Ahmed, who teaches English at a government primary school in a remote village on Bangladesh's border with India, where most parents are farmers and many children miss school to work.

It follows his path from an English literature degree to teaching and training other teachers, and the approach that runs through it: a warm relationship with pupils, stories and songs every day, and games in place of the memorisation his pupils were used to. As a college lecturer his students twice had the highest pass rates in the district; his biggest lesson from teacher training was that English classes can be taught in English.

items.definition: English Teaching Forum, Volume 61, Number 1 (2023), U.S. Department of State
Kathuli Government Primary School, Meherpur District, Bangladesh

blocks.heading: How it works
numbered: **Build the relationship first** - stories, folktales and songs every day, and activities outside class such as sport, art and music.
**Replace memorisation with play:** word games, guessing games and chain stories get pupils speaking without a script.
**Use short, lively activities** with weak classes - a jazz chant, a running dictation, a picture chain drill.
**Teach in English.** His training showed him that an English class can be run in English, and he has taught that way since.

blocks.heading: In a Sri Lankan classroom
text: Almost everything in it will be familiar to a teacher in a rural Sri Lankan school: children who work before and after school, a mandated syllabus, parents who cannot help with English, and a strong habit of learning by heart.

It is not a method to copy step by step. It is a reminder, from a classroom very like ours, of what a single committed teacher can do - and a good text for a staff meeting or a teacher-training session.

blocks.heading: Try this tomorrow
items: Start one lesson this week with a short chant or story instead of a revision question.
